extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media scholars, and news professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and routines journalists and news organizations use to select, structure, and present news (news values, objectivity procedures, story forms, organizational constraints). Useful for evaluating newsworthiness and newsroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence/importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of a story is measured in its impact: how many lives it affects. Fatalities are more important than property damage. Actions of the powerful are newsworthy because what the powerful do affects the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use impact as a yardstick for newsworthiness; policy actions and events affecting large numbers of people rank higher. Emphasize outcomes that affect the public directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: People are interested in things that don't have a direct effect on their lives: celebrities, political gossip, and human dramas. Stories with a human element elicit this kind of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate issues through affected people (especially in television). Humanizing detail and personal narratives increase audience appeal even when policy significance is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict/controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict signals important issues and is inherently more interesting than harmony. Controversy alerts audiences to issues needing attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories around disputes, clashes, or opposing positions to heighten perceived newsworthiness. Be aware this prioritizes confrontation over consensus or nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The unusual
rubrics_metrics.description: The unusual captures attention because it deviates from the norm; audiences expect day-to-day regularity so exceptions are noteworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight anomalies and unexpected events. This criterion explains coverage of rare or sensational incidents even when they lack broader significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: News is timely. Because audience attention is limited, journalists prioritize what is happening now. Timely events are also more likely to require action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize recent or immediate developments; schedule stories so they coincide with newsday deadlines. Timeliness often drives selection even when depth suffers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that happen near are considered more newsworthy. Local events usually have more effect than distant ones; local angles are sought in national stories to interest audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find or create local hooks for broader stories. Geographic closeness increases perceived relevance and coverage likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: News judgment (use of agreed-on news values)
rubrics_metrics.description: News judgment is the ability to evaluate stories based on agreed-on news values, providing yardsticks of newsworthiness and directing consistent story selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the set of news values (prominence, human interest, conflict, unusualness, timeliness, proximity) to prioritize coverage; this is a routinized, audience-oriented decision tool rather than continuous audience consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity routine (defensive procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity is practiced as a routine set of procedures protecting journalists and organizations from attack (libel suits, criticism). Procedures include relying on verifiable facts, setting statements off in quotation marks, including many names, presenting supplementary evidence, attributing statements to sources, and reporting conflicting statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow verification and attribution practices to fend off criticism. Note limitations: attributing claims protects reporters legally but can propagate falsehoods; reliance on source claims without verification can produce distorted coverage (e.g., McCarthy era reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of mobilizing information
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of objectivity, news routines often omit mobilizing information (instructions on what to do, where to go, times) especially if material is negative, controversial, nonlocal, or on main/news/editorial pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including action-oriented or advocacy details to reduce accusations of partisanship; this practice can limit the public's ability to act on information and can be an anti-pattern for public-interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation techniques and audience appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Content must be presented to meet audience needs: readable stories, properly arranged photos, headlines composed to direct attention, and visually appealing television messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use layout, headlines, visuals, and concise writing to hold audience attention. Presentation routines shape what facts are included and how they are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story structure (narrative/dramatic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dominant routine is to structure news as a story with attributes of fiction/drama: structure and conflict, problem and denouement, rising action and falling action, a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame reports as narratives to increase engagement ('tell stories, not reports'). Beware distortion: forcing complex or ongoing issues into neat plots can omit context or contrary evidence (example: CBS documentary and failure to pursue contrary information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefined angles and reporter scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters often approach assignments with predefined options or scripts about what is significant, leading them to seek supportive sources and details that fit the angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of confirmation bias: anticipate scripts can lead to leading questions, selection of predictable sources, and constrained coverage (examples: freeway story Q&A; crew filming self-immolation incident). Seek diverse sources and contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event routine and the event 'peg'
rubrics_metrics.description: News routines favor discrete events as defensible news items. Events serve as pegs for issues and provide schedules and visual material (especially for TV). The media often prefer stories with a clear location, victim, drama, and finite lifespan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use timely events as hooks for broader issues, but recognize that the event model can marginalize long-term, systemic problems lacking compact event structure (e.g., chronic public-health issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard news vs. soft news classification (scheduling-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news is usually tied to prescheduled or unscheduled events that must be reported quickly; soft news (features) is nonscheduled and can be carried at the organization's convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and schedule content accordingly. Understand that this distinction is organizational (based on scheduling) rather than solely substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational production routines and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational routines (wire service menus, beats, bureaus, deadlines, fixed news holes) structure what can be covered and how; they aim to ensure a steady, predictable product and reduce the range of choices for gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how source feeds (AP/wire) and beat assignments channel story proportions and limit novelty. Deadlines create temporal gaps and favor coincident/convenient news; beats and bureaus concentrate coverage on institutional sources and locations likely to generate news.
